tooley.q: Which computer bus is used to specify memory locations:
tooley.explain: The address bus carries the address of the memory location or device to be accessed.
tooley.detail: The three buses in a computer system each carry a distinct role: the address bus carries the location (one direction only, from the CPU outward), the data bus carries the actual data (bidirectional), and the control bus carries timing and control signals such as read/write, interrupts and clock pulses. Keeping each bus's role straight avoids confusion when reading a microprocessor system block diagram.

tooley.q: What is the largest hexadecimal address that can appear on a 24-bit address bus:
tooley.explain: 24 bits = 6 hex digits, and the largest value is all 1s → FFFFFF.
tooley.detail: Each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits, so an n-bit bus needs n/4 hex digits to write its highest address (when every bit is 1). With 24 bits, 24/4=6 hex digits, and the maximum value with every bit set to 1 is FFFFFF, corresponding to 2²⁴−1=16,777,215 addresses.

tooley.q: Bus arbitration is required in order to:
opts: reduce errors due to noise and EMI
tooley.explain: Bus arbitration decides which device may use the bus at any one time, preventing several devices from transmitting together.
tooley.detail: When several devices (the CPU, memory, peripheral controllers, and so on) share the same physical bus, only one device may be allowed to drive the bus at any given moment; otherwise, their electrical signals would overlap, causing bus contention and corrupting the data on the bus. A bus arbiter grants bus access according to a predetermined priority scheme.

tooley.q: A memory device in which any item of data can be retrieved with equal ease is known as:
tooley.explain: This is the definition of random-access memory (RAM/ROM in terms of physical nature).
tooley.detail: The name 'random access' is sometimes misleading because it only describes the ACCESS PATTERN, not whether the memory can be written to: any memory cell is reached just as quickly regardless of its location, unlike sequential-access media such as magnetic tape, which must be wound through cell by cell to reach the target one. Under this technical definition, both RAM and ROM are random-access memory, even though ROM cannot be written to.

tooley.q: Which one of the following memory devices can be erased and reprogrammed:
tooley.explain: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) is erased with UV light and can be reprogrammed many times; OTP can be written only once and Mask ROM is fixed at manufacture.
tooley.detail: The three ROM types in this question form an increasing scale of changeability: Mask ROM is etched permanently at the factory and can never be altered; OTP EPROM lets the user write to it exactly once using a programmer device; and UV EPROM can be erased by shining ultraviolet light through a quartz window on the chip's package, then reprogrammed many times over.

tooley.q: The processor instruction HLT is classed as:
tooley.explain: HLT halts the CPU and belongs to the group of instructions that control the processor's operation.
tooley.detail: A microprocessor's instruction set typically splits into a few main groups: data-transfer instructions (MOV, LOAD, and so on), arithmetic/logic instructions (ADD, AND, and so on), and control instructions that govern execution flow or the CPU's own state (JMP, HLT, and so on). HLT moves or computes no data at all; it simply tells the CPU to stop its fetch-execute cycle, which places it squarely in the control instruction group.

tooley.q: The VME bus standard uses:
tooley.explain: The VMEbus standard uses two DIN 41612 connectors (P1 and P2), each with 32 rows of pins.
tooley.detail: VMEbus is a widely used backplane bus standard in industrial and aerospace systems, letting several cards plug into one chassis and share the same bus system. Each VMEbus card connects to the backplane through two separate DIN 41612 connectors called P1 and P2, each with 32 rows of pins, together providing enough signal lines for the address, data and control buses combined.

tooley.q: What type of memory uses the principle of charge storage:
tooley.explain: DRAM (MOS dynamic memory) stores data as charge on the capacitor of each cell and needs periodic refresh.
tooley.detail: A DRAM cell is essentially just a tiny capacitor together with a transistor acting as a switch to charge or discharge it. Because a capacitor naturally leaks its charge over time, every cell must be read and rewritten (refreshed) periodically, typically every few milliseconds, or the stored data will gradually fade away even while power stays continuously applied.

tooley.q: How many 16K×4-bit DRAM devices are required to provide 32K bytes of storage:
tooley.explain: 16K×4bit = 8KB/chip; 32KB ÷ 8KB = 4 chip.
tooley.detail: A memory chip's capacity equals its number of words multiplied by the bits per word, then divided by 8 to convert to bytes. A 16K×4-bit chip holds 16,384×4=65,536 bits, which is 8,192 bytes (8KB). To reach a total of 32KB, enough chips must be combined in parallel so their byte capacities add up to 32KB, which is 32÷8=4 chips.

tooley.q: A memory device has a pin marked CAS. The function of this pin is:
tooley.explain: CAS = Column Address Select, used in DRAM to latch the column address portion.
tooley.detail: To save on package pins, DRAM splits a memory address into two halves sent sequentially over the same set of address pins: the row half is latched by the RAS (Row Address Select) signal, then the column half is latched by the CAS (Column Address Select) signal. This address-multiplexing technique lets DRAM use far fewer pins than sending the whole address at once would require.

tooley.q: A semiconductor memory consisting of 256 rows and 256 columns has a capacity of:
tooley.detail: A memory array is organised as a row-column grid, so its total capacity equals the number of rows multiplied by the number of columns. With 256 rows and 256 columns, the total number of memory cells (each storing 1 bit) is 256×256=65,536, and since 1K in a memory context conventionally means 1,024 (=2¹⁰), 65,536÷1,024=64, so the capacity is written compactly as 64K bits.

tooley.q: In the assembly language instruction MOV AX, 07FEh, the operation code is:
tooley.explain: MOV is the operation code (opcode); AX is the destination register and 07FEh is the data operand.
tooley.detail: A typical assembly instruction has two parts: the operation code (opcode, here MOV) specifying what action the CPU must perform, and the operands (here AX and 07FEh) specifying what that action acts upon. The same MOV opcode can appear with many different operand combinations, but the word 'MOV' itself always keeps the role of the opcode.

tooley.q: The stack is used for:
tooley.explain: The stack temporarily stores return addresses and register values during function calls/interrupts.
tooley.detail: The stack works on a last-in, first-out (LIFO) principle, which suits storing values that must be restored in reverse order later, most typically the return address when calling a subroutine or handling an interrupt. When the subroutine finishes, the value on top of the stack is popped so the CPU returns to exactly the point where it had paused.

tooley.q: The stack is a structure located:
tooley.explain: The stack is an area of external RAM managed by the stack pointer (SP).
tooley.detail: The stack is not a separate piece of hardware; it is simply an ordinary region of external RAM, managed by a special register called the stack pointer (SP), which always points to the stack's current top. Every push or pop instruction simply reads from or writes to whichever memory cell SP is currently pointing at, then increments or decrements SP.

tooley.q: A byte of data is to be inverted. This task is performed by:
tooley.explain: Bit inversion (NOT) is a logic operation performed by the ALU.
tooley.detail: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) is the one block inside the CPU dedicated to performing arithmetic operations (add, subtract, and so on) and logic operations (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, and so on) on data. Inverting a byte is simply applying NOT to each bit, so this is always the ALU's job, not the instruction register's or the instruction decoder's, which only hold and analyse the instruction code.

tooley.q: The output of the instruction pointer appears on:
tooley.explain: The instruction pointer/PC holds the address of the next instruction and places it on the address bus so the CPU can fetch the instruction.
tooley.detail: Before the CPU can fetch an instruction from memory, it must know exactly which address that instruction sits at. The instruction pointer, also called the Program Counter, holds that address and places it on the address bus at the start of every fetch cycle, so memory returns the correct instruction byte over the data bus.

tooley.q: The CPU data bus buffer is:
tooley.explain: The data bus must carry data in both directions (read and write), so the buffer must be bidirectional.
tooley.detail: Unlike the address bus, which only travels one way outward from the CPU, the data bus must carry data in both directions: the CPU reads data in from memory or a device, and the CPU writes data out to memory or a device. The buffer connecting the CPU to the data bus must therefore be bidirectional, able to switch direction depending on whether the current instruction is a read or a write.

tooley.q: Another way to describe the CPU register that acts as an instruction pointer is:
tooley.explain: The Program Counter (PC) is simply another name for the instruction pointer.
tooley.detail: Different microprocessor manufacturers sometimes use different names for the same functional register. 'Instruction pointer' and 'Program Counter' refer to exactly the same single register, the one holding the address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed; only the name differs depending on the documentation or specific CPU architecture.

tooley.q: In which cycle is an instruction fetched and decoded:
tooley.explain: As the book describes it, machine cycle M1 is the opcode fetch cycle (fetch and decode of the instruction).
tooley.detail: A machine instruction executes over several successive machine cycles, each handling a different stage. The M1 cycle is always the first, fixed cycle of EVERY instruction: the CPU places the address from PC onto the address bus, receives the opcode from memory over the data bus, then decodes that opcode to know what further steps the following cycles must carry out.

tooley.q: If a microprocessor clock runs at 50MHz, an instruction requiring 11 T-states will execute in a time of:
tooley.explain: Clock period T = 1/50MHz = 20ns; 11 T-states × 20ns = 220ns.
tooley.detail: A T-state is the smallest unit of time inside a CPU, equal to exactly one clock cycle. To find an instruction's real execution time, first convert the clock frequency to a period (T=1/f), then multiply by the number of T-states the instruction needs. At 50MHz, each T-state lasts 1/50,000,000 second = 20ns; an instruction needing 11 T-states takes 11×20ns=220ns to complete.

tooley.q: An external device can gain the attention of the CPU by generating a signal on the:
tooley.explain: IRQ (Interrupt Request) is the standard signal line by which a peripheral asks the CPU to service an interrupt.
tooley.detail: Rather than forcing the CPU to continuously poll every peripheral to see which one needs attention, most microprocessors dedicate a signal line called IRQ (Interrupt Request) that lets a peripheral actively signal when it needs the CPU to pause its current work and service it right away. This is far more efficient than polling when several devices need a fast response but are not continuously active.

tooley.q: When executing the instruction MOV AX, 07FEh, the operation code will be transferred to:
tooley.explain: After being fetched, the opcode is placed in the instruction register (IR) to be decoded.
tooley.detail: Once the CPU fetches an instruction byte from memory over the data bus, that byte is not processed on the spot; it is moved into the Instruction Register (IR) to be held steady throughout decoding, since the data bus itself may already be reused for something else, such as fetching the next operand, right afterward.

tooley.q: After executing MOV AX, 07FEh, the binary data in the AL register will be:
tooley.explain: The 16-bit AX consists of AH (high byte) and AL (low byte); 07FEh → AH = 07h, AL = FEh = 11111110₂.
tooley.detail: In the x86 architecture, the 16-bit AX register splits into two separately addressable 8-bit halves: AH (the upper byte) and AL (the lower byte). The value 07FEh written out as 16 bits is 0000 0111 1111 1110; splitting it in half, the upper 07h loads into AH and the lower FEh loads into AL, and FEh in binary is 11111110.

tooley.q: The advantage of pipelining is:
tooley.explain: Pipelining overlaps the instruction-processing stages, increasing execution throughput.
tooley.detail: Without pipelining, a CPU must complete all the fetch, decode and execute steps of one instruction before starting the next. With pipelining, while instruction A is in its execute stage, the next instruction B can already be in its decode stage, and instruction C after it can be starting fetch, all overlapping within the same clock cycles, considerably increasing how many instructions complete per unit of time even though each individual instruction still takes the same number of steps.

tooley.q: Segmentation is used with x86 processors in order to:
tooley.explain: Segmentation combines segment + offset so a 16-bit CPU can address a memory area larger than a pure 16-bit register allows.
tooley.detail: A plain 16-bit register can directly address at most 2¹⁶=65,536 bytes (64KB). Segmentation gets around this limit by combining two 16-bit registers, a segment and an offset, using the formula physical address = segment×16 + offset, which reaches an address space of up to 1MB even though each individual register still holds only 16 bits.

tooley.q: The main constituents of a computer are:
tooley.explain: The 4 main blocks of a complete computer system: CPU (processing), ROM (fixed program memory), RAM (temporary memory), I/O (input/output).

tooley.q: The integrated circuits shown in Figure A2.7 are:
tooley.explain: The '27xxx' marking is the standard naming convention for UV-erasable EPROMs (UV-EPROM).

tooley.q: The number of individual addresses that can be addressed by a processor that has a 16-bit address bus is:
tooley.explain: 2¹⁶ = 65,536 different addresses.

tooley.q: In a static memory circuit:
opts: retained indefinitely (as long as power is applied)
needs to be refreshed continuously even while power is applied
lost as soon as power is removed
tooley.explain: SRAM holds its data stably for as long as power is applied and does NOT need a refresh cycle like DRAM (but it still loses data if power is removed: this is the difference between 'retained indefinitely' and 'non-volatile').

tooley.q: How many 16K×4-bit DRAM devices are needed to provide 64K bytes of storage:
tooley.explain: 16K×4bit = 8KB/chip; 64KB ÷ 8KB = 8 chip.

tooley.q: Bus arbitration is required in order to:
opts: reduce errors due to noise and EMI
tooley.explain: Bus arbitration decides which device may use the bus, preventing several devices from transmitting at once and causing a conflict (bus contention).

tooley.q: The clock oscillator in a microprocessor system provides:
opts: a train of rectangular pulses from a free-running oscillator
tooley.explain: A standard clock oscillator produces a frequency-stable square wave to synchronise the whole system.

tooley.q: In a microprocessor system, faster processing can be achieved by means of:
tooley.explain: Instruction pipelining overlaps the fetch/decode/execute stages of several instructions, increasing throughput.

tooley.q: A computer has 2K bytes of RAM. How many 32-bit words can be stored in this memory?
tooley.explain: 2K bytes = 2048 bytes; each 32-bit word = 4 bytes; 2048÷4 = 512 words.

tooley.q: Which one of the following describes the function of a ROM in a computer system?
opts: temporary storage of programs and data
permanent storage of programs and data
tooley.explain: ROM is read-only memory that keeps its data when power is lost → permanent storage of fixed programs/data.

tooley.q: When a computer is first initialised, the code responsible for performing bootstrap operations is stored in:
tooley.explain: The bootstrap code must exist before RAM is loaded with data → it is stored in ROM (usually flash ROM/BIOS).

floyd.q: A nibble consists of eight bits.
floyd.explain: A nibble = 4 bits; 8 bits is 1 byte, not a nibble.
floyd.detail: The bit, nibble and byte units form a fixed hierarchy: 1 nibble = 4 bits, 1 byte = 2 nibbles = 8 bits. Confusing a nibble with a byte is a very common mistake since both are small multiples of a bit; remembering the number 4 for a nibble helps avoid it.

floyd.q: A memory cell can store a byte of data.
floyd.explain: A memory cell stores only 1 BIT; 8 cells are needed to store 1 byte.
floyd.detail: A 'memory cell' in digital memory terminology always refers to the SMALLEST storage unit, exactly 1 bit (0 or 1). To store a complete byte, a ROW of 8 such cells working together is needed, not a single cell.

floyd.q: The location of a unit of data in a memory array is called its address.
floyd.explain: True by the standard definition.
floyd.detail: An address is the unique 'coordinate' identifying a data unit's location within the entire memory array, much like a house number identifies a location on a street. Without an address, the CPU would have no way of knowing exactly where to read from or write to.

floyd.q: A data bus is bidirectional in operation.
floyd.explain: True: the data bus can both read and write, unlike the address bus (one-way).
floyd.detail: The data bus needs to carry data in both directions because the CPU both READS data in from memory and WRITES data out to memory. The address bus is quite different: it always flows in exactly ONE direction, outward from the CPU, since only the CPU ever needs to specify an address, with no reverse direction needed.

floyd.q: RAM is a random address memory.
floyd.explain: RAM = Random ACCESS Memory, not 'random address'.
floyd.detail: This is a fairly common mix-up of the acronym's expansion. The A in RAM stands for ACCESS, describing how every cell is reached equally quickly regardless of location, not ADDRESS. Confusing these two words makes RAM's definition meaningless.

floyd.q: Data stored in a static RAM is retained even after power is removed.
floyd.explain: SRAM is still volatile memory: it loses its data when power is removed, just like DRAM.
floyd.detail: 'Static' in SRAM only means it does NOT need periodic refreshing the way DRAM does; it has nothing to do with retaining data when power is removed. Both SRAM and DRAM belong to the volatile memory category, quite unlike ROM or flash, which are nonvolatile.

floyd.q: Cache is a type of memory used for intermediate or temporary storage of data.
floyd.explain: True: cache temporarily holds frequently used data/instructions to speed up access.
floyd.detail: Cache exploits the principle that 'recently used data tends to be used again': it keeps a temporary copy of data or instructions the CPU has just accessed in a small but very fast memory, so a repeated access does not have to wait for the much slower main memory.

floyd.q: Dynamic RAMs must be periodically refreshed to retain data.
floyd.explain: True: DRAM stores data as charge on a capacitor, which leaks, so it needs refreshing.
floyd.detail: A DRAM cell is just a tiny capacitor, and a capacitor naturally LEAKS its charge over time even with no load drawing current from it. Without periodic read-and-rewrite (refresh), each cell would gradually lose its charge and the data would become corrupted, even while the main power supply stays continuously on.

floyd.q: ROM is a read-only memory.
floyd.explain: True by definition/name.
floyd.detail: The name ROM (Read-Only Memory) accurately describes its limitation: the CPU can only READ data out of it, never WRITE new data into it during normal operation. In exchange, ROM retains its data permanently even when power is removed, unlike RAM.

floyd.q: A flash memory uses a flashing beam of light to store data.
floyd.explain: Flash memory stores data as charge in a semiconductor floating gate, unrelated to light.
floyd.detail: The name 'flash' has NOTHING to do with light; it comes from how quickly the memory can be ERASED, like a 'flash', compared with earlier EEPROM technology, which erased one byte at a time much more slowly. The underlying storage mechanism still relies on charge trapped in an insulated floating gate layer, the same principle as EPROM/EEPROM.

floyd.q: Registers are at the top of a memory hierarchy.
floyd.explain: True: registers are the fastest, located right inside the CPU, at the top of the memory hierarchy.
floyd.detail: The memory hierarchy arranges memory types along an axis of decreasing speed and increasing capacity: registers (fastest, smallest, right inside the CPU), then cache, then main RAM, then external storage (hard disk, SSD). The higher up the hierarchy, the faster the access but the higher the cost per bit.

floyd.q: Cloud storage is accessed through the Internet.
floyd.explain: True by definition.
floyd.detail: Cloud storage is really data kept on a PHYSICAL server at a remote data center, accessed by the user over an Internet connection instead of plugging a drive directly into their own machine. The 'cloud' is just a figurative name; the data still physically resides on real hardware somewhere.

floyd.q: The bit capacity of a memory that has 512 addresses and can store 8 bits at each address is
floyd.detail: A memory's total capacity is always the number of addresses MULTIPLIED by the bits stored at each address, much like total storage equals the number of drawers multiplied by each drawer's capacity. With 512 addresses at 8 bits each, the total capacity is 512×8=4096 bits.

floyd.q: A 16-bit word consists of
floyd.explain: 16 bit ÷ 4 bit/nibble = 4 nibble.
floyd.detail: Converting between the bit, nibble and byte units just needs dividing by their fixed ratio: 1 nibble = 4 bits. A 16-bit word divided by 4 gives exactly 4 nibbles, equivalent to 2 bytes.

floyd.q: Data are stored in a random-access memory (RAM) during the
floyd.explain: Write is the operation that stores NEW data in RAM.
floyd.detail: RAM has exactly two opposite basic operations: READ, which retrieves existing data without changing it, and WRITE, which places NEW data in, overwriting whatever was previously at that address. Only the write operation actually STORES new data into memory.

floyd.q: Data that are stored at a given address in a RAM are lost when
opts: the data are read from the address
new data are written at the address
floyd.explain: Losing power (RAM is volatile) OR being overwritten by new data both destroy the old data.
floyd.detail: Data in RAM can disappear for two entirely different reasons: RAM's inherently VOLATILE nature (losing power erases everything), or the data being deliberately OVERWRITTEN by new data at that same address. The READ operation, on the other hand, never erases data, since reading only retrieves a value without altering the cell's content.

floyd.q: A ROM is a
floyd.explain: ROM keeps its data permanently even when power is lost: it is nonvolatile.
floyd.detail: The most important property distinguishing ROM from RAM is being NONVOLATILE: once data has been loaded into ROM, typically during manufacturing or one-time programming, it remains intact even with the power completely removed, unlike RAM, which loses everything the instant power is cut.

floyd.q: A memory with 512 addresses has
floyd.explain: 512 = 2⁹ → 9 address lines are needed to encode 512 different addresses.
floyd.detail: The NUMBER OF ADDRESS LINES needed always relates to the maximum number of addresses through the formula 2ⁿ, where n is the number of address lines. To encode 512 distinct addresses, n must satisfy 2ⁿ=512, and since 2⁹=512, the answer is 9 address lines.

floyd.q: A byte-organized memory has
floyd.explain: 1 byte = 8 bits → 8 data output lines are needed to read or write one byte in parallel.
floyd.detail: 'Byte-organized' means the memory reads or writes a whole byte in ONE access, not bit by bit. Since a byte is exactly 8 bits, exactly 8 parallel data lines are needed to carry all 8 bits in or out at the same time.

floyd.q: The storage element of a DRAM is a
floyd.explain: DRAM stores data as charge on a tiny capacitor.
floyd.detail: A DRAM cell's physical structure is just one tiny capacitor plus one transistor acting as a switch, far simpler than an SRAM cell, which typically needs 6 transistors. This simplicity is what lets DRAM achieve much higher storage density than SRAM on the same chip area, at the cost of needing periodic refresh.

floyd.q: ADDRESS-BURST is a feature of
floyd.explain: According to the book, ADDRESS-BURST is the name of a specific pin/feature of synchronous SRAM presented in this chapter.
floyd.detail: Burst mode allows several CONSECUTIVE addresses to be accessed with just ONE initial address supplied, then automatically incrementing on each clock pulse, speeding up large block data transfers. This feature is tied to SYNCHRONOUS memory types (synchronised to the system clock), unlike asynchronous memory, which handles each access independently.

floyd.q: In a computer, the BIOS programs are stored in the
floyd.explain: The BIOS must survive power loss → it is stored in ROM (usually flash ROM).
floyd.detail: BIOS must be ready to run IMMEDIATELY when the computer powers on, before RAM has even been loaded with any data, so it must reside in a memory type that does NOT lose its contents when the machine is off, that is, ROM (typically flash ROM so the firmware can still be updated later).

floyd.q: SRAM, DRAM, flash, and EEPROM are all
floyd.explain: All 4 types are semiconductor memory.
floyd.detail: Despite differing storage mechanisms (a capacitor for DRAM, a latch circuit for SRAM, a floating gate for flash/EEPROM), all four are fabricated on a silicon semiconductor base, quite unlike magnetic storage technologies (hard disks) or optical ones (CD/DVD discs).

floyd.q: Optical storage devices employ
floyd.explain: CD/DVD/Blu-ray use a laser to read and write data.
floyd.detail: Optical storage devices encode data as different light-reflecting spots (pits/lands) on a disc surface, then use a tightly focused laser beam to read back that reflectance difference. Blu-ray technology uses a shorter-wavelength laser than CD/DVD, allowing a smaller focused spot and much higher storage density.

floyd.q: Memory latency is
opts: time to reference a block of data
floyd.explain: By the book's definition, memory latency is measured from the viewpoint of the processor's access time to memory.
floyd.detail: 'Latency' in digital systems generally always means the DELAY before a request gets serviced. For memory, the book specifically defines it as the time the processor must WAIT from issuing an access request until it actually receives the data back from memory, not other concepts such as hit rate or downtime.

floyd.q: A facility that houses a cloud storage system is called a
floyd.explain: The standard term is 'data center'.
floyd.detail: A 'data center' is a dedicated physical facility housing thousands of servers, cooling systems, and backup power to run cloud storage services continuously around the clock. This is the standard industry term, unlike the playful 'cloud house' phrasing, which is not an actual technical term.

generated.q: A microprocessor with a 32-bit address bus can directly address up to:
